verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them, ‘A priest shall not defile himself for the dead among his people;
except for his relatives that are near to him: for his mother, for his father, for his son, for his daughter, for his brother,
and for his virgin sister who is near to him, who has had no husband; for her he may defile himself.
He shall not defile himself, being a chief man among his people, to profane himself.
“‘They shall not shave their heads or shave off the corners of their beards or make any cuttings in their flesh.
They shall be holy to their God, and not profane the name of their God; for they offer the offerings of Yahweh made by fire, the bread of their God; therefore they shall be holy.
“‘They shall not marry a woman who is a prostitute, or profane. They shall not marry a woman divorced from her husband; for he is holy to his God.
You shall sanctify him therefore; for he offers the bread of your God. He shall be holy to you; for I Yahweh, who sanctify you, am holy.
“‘The daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by playing the prostitute, she profanes her father. She shall be burned with fire.

“‘He who is the high priest among his brothers, upon whose head the anointing oil is poured, and that is consecrated to put on the garments, shall not let the hair of his head hang loose, or tear his clothes.
He must not go in to any dead body, or defile himself for his father, or for his mother.
He shall not go out of the sanctuary, nor profane the sanctuary of his God; for the crown of the anointing oil of his God is upon him. I am Yahweh.
“‘He shall take a wife in her virginity.
A widow, or one divorced, or a woman who has been defiled, or a prostitute, these he shall not marry: but a virgin of his own people shall he take as a wife.
He shall not profane his offspring  among his people, for I am Yahweh who sanctifies him.’”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Say to Aaron, ‘None of your offspring  throughout their generations who has a defect may approach to offer the bread of his God.
For whatever man he is that has a defect, he shall not draw near: a blind man, or a lame, or he who has a flat nose, or any deformity,
or a man who has an injured foot, or an injured hand,
or hunchbacked, or a dwarf, or one who has a defect in his eye, or an itching disease, or scabs, or who has damaged testicles.

No man of the offspring  of Aaron the priest who has a defect shall come near to offer the offerings of Yahweh made by fire. Since he has a defect, he shall not come near to offer the bread of his God.
He shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy.
He shall not come near to the veil, nor come near to the altar, because he has a defect; that he may not profane my sanctuaries, for I am Yahweh who sanctifies them.’”
So Moses spoke to Aaron, and to his sons, and to all the children of Israel.

footnotes.content: The priest has a calling set apart—a threshold not to cross, even for grief. The Lord guards His servants' focus: they belong first to Him, then to the people. In our own way, we too are invited to cherish what He has set apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the Lord draws a circle of mercy within the law: the nearest kin matter. Even in holiness, family love is honored. Our closest bonds—mother, father, child, sibling—are not worldly pull but sacred trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A virgin sister under his roof is under his care, and the Lord names that as worthy reason to break the rule. Tenderness within duty—the mark of a heart shaped by God's own care for the unprotected.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the chief among priests must not use rank to blur the boundary. Holiness is not a loophole; it's a choice made daily, in small obediences. The higher the place, the straighter the walk.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The customs of pagan mourning—shaved heads, torn beards, ritual scars—are forbidden. This tells us something: the Lord wants His priests freed from old patterns, not mimicking the nations. He calls them to new ways, marked by His presence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Holiness is not hidden; it shows in how we live and speak. The priest handles the Lord's own bread, speaks His name—these are not small things. Every action echoes. We too are sanctified for a purpose; the world watches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest's marriage is part of his holiness—a covenant the Lord cares about. A wife met in wholeness, not shame, carries a man's faithfulness into his household and his work. Marriage matters to God's ordering of His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest is sanctified for others' sake, not his own glory. The whole people shall honor him—not because he is great, but because through him the Lord draws near. He bears a weight of holiness that belongs to the One who sent him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When a priest's daughter turns to shameful paths, her father's name is dragged with her—and the law is swift and severe. This is hard mercy: it teaches that holiness is a family trust, and betrayal has weight. It also warns us how our choices touch those we love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high priest's oil-anointing marks him as set apart for all. Even in sorrow, he shall not let his hair hang loose or tear his garments—his restraint is a sign to the people that the Lord's work goes on. Grief is real, but the post is not abandoned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high priest's holiness is so complete that even the death of his own parents cannot draw him to ritual defilement. This seems harsh—and it teaches us that the Lord's work and the Lord's presence are above all else, even love for those who gave us life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high priest must stay in the sanctuary—protected in holiness, yes, but also confined to it. The crown of anointing oil is his highest honor and his deepest bind. Nearness to the Holy comes with a call to dwell there, not roam.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high priest's wife comes to him in her virginity—whole and unbroken. This speaks to God's delight in beginnings unmarked by shame. In the Lord's ordering, first unions matter deeply; they are not mere custom but covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Widow, divorced woman, defiled woman, prostitute—all are named and all are forbidden. This is not cruelty; it is clarity about holiness. The high priest's household is the Lord's household, and He reserves the right to define what belongs in it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high priest's offspring carry forward the consecration—their very existence is bound to his holiness. Children are not accidents; they are heirs of a calling. What we do echoes in generations to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the high priest's rules, now Aaron's sons generally. The Lord speaks directly to Moses again, turning to the larger priesthood. Each layer of rule shows us the Lord's care for order and clarity in His house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No priest with a defect may approach the altar. This was harsh law in its time—and yet it reminds us: the Lord sees and knows every body, every imperfection. Before Him, there are no hidden flaws. The sanctuary itself bears witness to His omniscience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Blind man, lame, flat-nosed—the defects are named with plainness, no euphemism. The Lord is direct about what He requires for altar service. This law does not diminish a man's worth before God; it specifies a role. The two are not the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Injured foot, injured hand—wounds that limit movement and touch are listed. The priest's body is his tool: he must approach, handle, lift, serve. An injury that keeps him from that work keeps him from the altar. The rule flows from the task.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The list grows long and specific: hunchback, dwarf, eye defects, itching disease, scabs, damaged testicles. The Lord names the body's many ailments without shame. He is not embarrassed by our flesh; He made it. But the altar has a particularity all its own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The reason is repeated with weight: a defect bars the priest from the altar work itself. He is not diminished as a man, not cast out from the people—but a specific calling requires a specific readiness. The Lord does not negotiate about His house's particularity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet he shall eat of the bread—holy and most holy. The defected priest is not destitute or dishonored; he is fed from the sanctuary's own store. He bears a loss, yes, but the Lord makes provision. Grace and law stand together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He shall not draw near the veil or altar. His boundary is drawn, not in shame but in honor to the sanctuary itself. The sanctuary must be kept whole; one blemished approach could profane it. Separation here is protection—of the Holy, and of the priest's own standing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses delivers the word to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel. What is spoken becomes law; what is heard is now known. The whole people learn how their priest is set apart—and why. Covenant is not hidden; it is proclaimed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
